3b1e5706b8: Two rules keep wrappers correct. Accept anything: *args, **kwargs forwards whatever the caller passed, so the wrapper works on any signature. Return the result: return func(*args, **kwargs). Forgetting that return is the most common decorator bug. Every decorated function silently returns None, and the symptom shows up far from the cause.
b653685445: That __wrapped__ link matters beyond cosmetics. Introspection tools follow it: inspect.signature() sees through a wrapped function to the original's signature. Tracebacks still show the wrapper frames, and wraps cannot remove those. But debuggers and documentation tools can find the real function underneath.
9cbdf5b448: Something runs at import time. Code in the decorator body, outside the wrapper, runs when the def executes. Registration decorators use this on purpose (see Practice, Task 2). Anything else is usually a surprise. A decorator that opens files or network connections at import will do it on every import.
ad0ecf9198: Reach for a decorator when the same behavior wraps many functions unchanged: logging, timing, retry, caching, authentication checks. The reason is consolidation. You get one implementation, applied in one line, instead of the same lines copied into ten bodies.
d403e29459: And keep the composition honest. A decorator must return something the name can sensibly refer to. For functions, that means a callable. A decorator that returns None deletes the function by another name. The resulting TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable appears at the call site, a long way from the actual mistake.
37ff67d4ea: Terminology first. A descriptor is any object that defines __get__, __set__, or __delete__. These methods only have meaning when the object sits as a class attribute. Python calls them during attribute access on instances of that class.
2f8674ea1e: Assignment has a matching rule. obj.attr = value calls the data descriptor's __set__ if one exists; otherwise it writes the instance dictionary. So plain assignment can never shadow a data descriptor's attribute. The write always goes through the descriptor.
e625da1918: Two consequences you will meet in real code. A property is a data descriptor, so you cannot shadow it by assignment. obj.prop = x always goes through the property's setter, or raises if there is none. A method is a non-data descriptor, so you can shadow it per instance. obj.method = something replaces the method for that one instance only. That is monkey-patching, and the lookup rules are what make it possible.
a7b54bf1a8:
When does the descriptor win? When the logic is parameterized and reused. Bounded(10, 30) and Bounded(0, 100) are two uses of one class. A property cannot take parameters, so you would copy the validation into every class that needs it. The rule of thumb:

  • one class, one attribute → property;
  • same logic in several places, or logic that needs configuration → descriptor.
fd984d5101: The wrapper needs somewhere to keep the count. An attribute on the wrapper itself is the natural place. The closure gives each decorated function its own wrapper, so each gets its own counter.
b1352a3ddb: This is the standard plugin-registration pattern. Frameworks from pytest to Flask extensions collect callables this way. Decoration is enrollment, and the registry gets read later, when it is time to run things.
